paragraphs.title: A Plea Amid Illness and Suffering

answers: Rebuke and chasten him in anger
easy.explanation: He asks, “O LORD, rebuke me not in thy wrath: neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask the LORD not to do?

answers: As afflicted with wounds, disease, and pain
easy.explanation: He says there is no soundness in his flesh and describes wounds, disease, weakness, and pain.
easy.q: How does the psalmist describe his physical condition?

easy.explanation: He says there is no rest in his bones because of his sin and that his iniquities are too heavy for him.
easy.q: What does the psalmist connect with his suffering?

medium.explanation: The image of a heavy burden shows that his iniquities are difficult for him to bear.
medium.q: What does the comparison to “an heavy burden” show about the psalmist’s iniquities?

medium.explanation: The word “stink” describes wounds that had become foul or corrupt.
medium.q: Which word means that the psalmist’s wounds had begun to decay or smell?

answers: From wounds and disease to weakness, pain, and inner distress
medium.explanation: The psalm moves through physical wounds, disease, weakness, mourning, and troubled inner feelings.
medium.q: How do the descriptions of suffering build through these verses?

answers: He sees prayer as a way to seek help in suffering
He is unaware of his condition
He is asking to take revenge on his enemies
challenge.explanation: Even while suffering, he directs his plea to the LORD for mercy and help.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the psalmist turning to God while describing his illness?

answers: The suffering is both physical and inward
The psalmist is speaking only about enemies
challenge.explanation: The passage describes bodily affliction as well as troubled emotions and the heart.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the movement from outward wounds to the disquietness of the heart?

answers: He describes a single brief event
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes the continual and lasting nature of his distress.
challenge.q: What does “all the day long” suggest about his mourning?

paragraphs.title: The Pain Is Visible Before God

answers: Only the words of his enemies
easy.explanation: He says, “Lord, all my desire is before thee; and my groaning is not hid from thee.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist say is before the LORD?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “my strength faileth me.”
easy.q: What happened to the psalmist’s strength?

easy.explanation: He says, “as for the light of mine eyes, it also is gone from me.”
easy.q: What happened to the light of his eyes?

answers: It shows that God knows his suffering without further explanation
It proves that his enemies have disappeared
medium.explanation: The psalmist trusts that God sees even his inward and unspoken distress.
medium.q: How does the fact that his groaning is not hidden strengthen his hope?

answers: His heart is troubled and restless
His heart is filled with celebration
medium.explanation: The expression portrays inward agitation and distress.

answers: Together they show widespread weakness affecting his whole life
Together they describe his enemies’ success
medium.explanation: The three descriptions show that his distress affects both body and inner life.
medium.q: What connection exists between his heart, strength, and eyesight?

answers: God does not know anything about his suffering
Even his quiet pain is visible to God
He hides his feelings from everyone
challenge.explanation: The statement emphasizes that God knows the psalmist’s inward pain.
challenge.q: What does “my groaning is not hid from thee” mean in context?

answers: He can rely on God’s knowledge of his condition
His enemies pray in his place
challenge.explanation: Because God sees his weakness, the psalmist can still appeal to Him.
challenge.q: Why does describing his weakness not cancel his prayer?

answers: God knows both what he longs for and what causes him pain
He is speaking only about physical needs
challenge.explanation: The verse includes both his inward desires and his sorrowful groaning.
challenge.q: What is suggested by placing “all my desire” beside “my groaning”?

easy.explanation: They “stand aloof from” his sore, while his kinsmen stand afar off.
easy.q: How do the psalmist’s lovers and friends stand?

easy.explanation: They lay snares, speak mischievous things, and imagine deceits.
easy.q: What do those seeking his life do?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “my kinsmen stand afar off.”

answers: His relatives remain distant while enemies plot against him
medium.explanation: Both the distance of his relatives and the hostility of his enemies deepen his isolation.
medium.q: How is a feeling of isolation created in this passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to hostile and harmful words spoken by those seeking his hurt.

answers: The kinsmen stand at a distance, while the enemies actively plot against him
The kinsmen plot, while the enemies help
medium.explanation: The kinsmen are distant, whereas the enemies lay snares and imagine deceits.
medium.q: What is the main contrast between the kinsmen and the enemies?

answers: The psalmist suffers both physically and in his relationships
His illness has been cured by his friends
His only problem is the speech of his enemies
challenge.explanation: The passage presents bodily suffering together with abandonment and opposition.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the combination of illness and social isolation?

challenge.explanation: Both expressions stress that those close to him are not coming near to help.

answers: They seek his life, speak harmfully, and devise deceit
challenge.explanation: The enemies actively oppose him through traps, speech, and schemes.
challenge.q: How do the enemies act beyond merely keeping their distance?

answers: He does not answer, like a deaf and dumb man
easy.explanation: He says he is like a deaf man who hears not and a dumb man who does not open his mouth.
easy.q: How does the psalmist respond to his enemies?

easy.explanation: He says, “For in thee, O LORD, do I hope.”
easy.q: In whom does the psalmist place his hope for an answer?

answers: That his enemies will rejoice over him
That his relatives will help him
easy.explanation: He asks to be heard lest his enemies rejoice when his foot slips.

answers: He is unable to answer and trusts God to hear him
He is silent because he cannot understand his enemies
medium.explanation: His silence reflects helplessness, while his hope rests in God’s response.
medium.q: How is the psalmist’s silence connected to both weakness and faith?

answers: He is near to stumbling or falling
He has already won a victory
medium.explanation: The expression presents him as unstable and close to falling.

answers: Both express ongoing danger and distress
medium.explanation: He feels that his fall is near and that his sorrow remains constantly before him.
medium.q: What connects the fear of enemy rejoicing with his continual sorrow?

answers: He leaves judgment and response in God’s hands
He asks his enemies to judge him
challenge.explanation: His silence is joined to confidence that the LORD will hear and respond.
challenge.q: What does the choice not to answer his enemies imply when the psalmist says he hopes in God?

answers: His pain remains constantly present in his awareness
His pain exists only while he sleeps
The pain belongs only to his enemies
challenge.explanation: The word “continually” emphasizes the lasting presence of his sorrow.
challenge.q: What does “my sorrow is continually before me” mean?

answers: The psalmist does not answer his enemies but asks God to hear him
He begins arguing with his enemies and then leaves
He stops believing and turns only to people
challenge.explanation: His inability or refusal to answer people leads him to depend on God’s hearing.
challenge.q: How does the passage move from silence to a plea for an answer?

easy.explanation: He says, “For I will declare mine iniquity.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist say he will declare?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will be sorry for my sin.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist say he is sorry for?

easy.explanation: The psalmist openly declares his iniquity and expresses sorrow for his sin.
easy.q: What attitude does this confession express?

answers: It reinforces the connection he sees between his suffering and sin
It cancels all his descriptions of suffering
It blames his suffering only on his friends
medium.explanation: By confessing his iniquity and sorrow for sin, he continues to connect his distress with wrongdoing.
medium.q: How does the confession relate to the earlier descriptions of suffering?
What does “iniquity” mean in this verse?

answers: He admits his sin and grieves over it
medium.explanation: The two statements combine confession with genuine sorrow.
medium.q: What is expressed by declaring iniquity and being sorry for sin?

answers: He considers his condition morally and spiritually as well as physically
He blames every person around him
challenge.explanation: His confession shows that he is examining his responsibility before God.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the psalmist focusing on his sin rather than only his pain?

answers: It makes the plea include acknowledgment of guilt, not merely a request for relief
It turns the plea into a song of victory
It removes the need to pray to God
challenge.explanation: The psalmist seeks help while openly recognizing his sin.
challenge.q: How does the confession change the nature of his plea?

answers: His sin does not matter to him
He thinks the sin belongs to his enemies
challenge.explanation: His sorrow shows that the sin is a serious source of inner distress.
challenge.q: What does being “sorry for my sin” indicate?

paragraphs.title: The Enemies’ Evil and the Plea for Salvation

easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “mine enemies are lively, and they are strong.”
easy.q: What happens to the psalmist’s enemies?

easy.explanation: They “render evil for good,” even though he follows what is good.
easy.q: How do those who hate the psalmist repay him?

answers: Not to forsake him and to hurry to help him
easy.explanation: He asks, “Forsake me not,” “be not far from me,” and “Make haste to help me.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask of the LORD at the end?

answers: They oppose him even though he follows what is good
He refuses to speak to them
They are merely far away from him
medium.explanation: They repay good with evil while he follows the thing that is good.
medium.q: Why is the enemies’ hatred presented as unjust?

medium.explanation: The phrase is an urgent request for God to come quickly to his aid.

answers: The illness and suffering lead to a request for God’s help and salvation
The psalm changes from prayer to a celebration of victory
The psalmist stops discussing his distress
medium.explanation: After describing suffering and enemies, he ends by asking God for help.
medium.q: How does the ending connect with the opening of the psalm?

answers: The enemies act unjustly toward someone pursuing goodness
The psalmist admits that he is the guilty enemy
The psalmist wants to repay evil with evil
challenge.explanation: The contrast presents the enemies’ response as undeserved and unjust.
challenge.q: What does the contrast between “evil for good” and “I follow the thing that good is” emphasize?

answers: A plea for God’s presence, nearness, and immediate assistance
A desire to move away from God
challenge.explanation: The three requests ask God not to abandon him, not to remain distant, and to help quickly.
challenge.q: What does the sequence “Forsake me not,” “be not far from me,” and “Make haste to help me” show?

answers: It identifies the LORD as the source of the psalmist’s rescue
It shows that the enemies have won
It returns to the description of his wounds
challenge.explanation: The psalm ends by identifying the LORD as the psalmist’s salvation.
challenge.q: Why is “O Lord my salvation” significant as the closing title for God?
